original_question: Is every continuous planar graph (1/2,3)-colourable, meaning that all points of the graph can be covered by radius-1/2 balls that can be colored with at most three colors so that any two intersecting balls receive different colors? Equivalently, can one prove that three colors always suffice, or exhibit a continuous planar graph that forces at least three colors and certify that lower bound?
target_in_paper: Section 3.3, unnumbered open problem "(1/2,3)-colorability of continuous planar graphs": "We conjecture that every continuous planar graph is (1/2,3)-colourable." ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the right open problem, the correct radius 1/2, the correct target of 3 colours, and the right collision rule for colours of intersecting balls, which is exactly the paper's Definition 11 of (r,c)-colourability specialized to r=1/2. Your request for a graph that provably needs at least 3 colours also matches the paper's nearby motivational remark, though not as an equivalent reformulation. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
missing_details: The paper's objects are continuous counterparts Γ(G) of combinatorial graphs G, obtained by replacing each edge of G with a unit-length continuous interval; to be fully stand-alone, the question should specify this model rather than say only "continuous planar graph." ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))

A ball B(p,1/2) is a metric ball in the continuous graph: the inclusion-maximal subgraph all of whose points lie at distance at most 1/2 from a center p, and the center p may be any point of the edge set E, not just an original vertex. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
The chosen balls must form a 1/2-cover of Γ, meaning every point q of the continuous graph lies in at least one selected ball. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))

The paper's standard parameter notation is χ_{1/2}(Γ), the minimum number of colours in such a 1/2-cover; the conjecture is exactly χ_{1/2}(Γ) ≤ 3 for planar Γ. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))

To stay closest to the paper's intent, planarity should be tied to the underlying combinatorial graph G (the paper motivates the question from loopless planar graphs and the continuous counterpart Γ(K4)); the paper does not separately formalize an independent topological definition of "continuous planar graph." This is an inference from its setup. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))

The sentence beginning "Equivalently" is not literally equivalent to the conjecture: exhibiting one planar continuous graph that requires at least 3 colours would only establish a lower bound and match the paper's heuristic side remark, not reformulate or resolve the universal 3-colourability conjecture. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
refined_question: Let G be a loopless planar combinatorial graph, and let Γ(G) denote its continuous counterpart in the sense of Definition 4, where each edge of G is replaced by a unit-length interval. Must Γ(G) be (1/2,3)-colourable; that is, does there always exist a family of balls B={B(p,1/2): p∈E(Γ(G))} whose union covers every point of Γ(G), together with a colouring f:B→{1,2,3}, such that whenever B,B'∈B have nonempty intersection, one has f(B)≠f(B')? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for every loopless planar graph G, is χ_{1/2}(Γ(G)) ≤ 3? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
justification: The draft is aimed at the Section 3.3 planar-colouring conjecture, not at the neighboring complete-graph question asking for χ_{1/2}(Γ(K_n)) and its upper bound in Proposition 2. The paper's official formulation is the unnumbered conjecture that every continuous planar graph is (1/2,3)-colourable, and the rest of the needed precision comes from Definitions 4, 8, 10, and 11. I therefore tightened the wording by making Γ(G), the unit-length edge model, the 1/2-cover condition, and the definition of the colouring constraint explicit, while removing the incorrect claim that the lower-bound example is equivalent to the conjecture. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14554))
